article_title: Growing syntactic structure and code-mixing in the weaker language: The Ivy Hypothesis
citation: Bernardini, P., & Schlyter, S. (2004). Growing syntactic structure and code-mixing in the weaker language: The Ivy Hypothesis. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 7(1), 49-69. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728904001270
title: The Ivy Hypothesis: code-mixing as gap-filling where higher syntactic structure comes from the stronger language
description: The Ivy Hypothesis proposes that in interactions meant to be in the weaker language, bilingual children with uneven development use portions of higher syntactic structure lexically instantiated in the stronger language combined with lower portions in the weaker language. The weaker language grows like ivy on the structural tree of the stronger language. The model is grounded in generative syntax within the Minimalist Program, assuming syntax is projected from the lexicon and that bilinguals have one universal syntax and two lexicons. It predicts that as the weaker language lexicon develops, successively higher portions of structure can be realized in that language, and mixing ceases once no functional gap remains.
requirements: A clear and consistent imbalance in syntactic development between the two languages, with one language clearly weaker throughout the acquisition period
constraints: The hypothesis is not claimed to be valid for all children with uneven development; less imbalance may lead to different mixing patterns, and some children do not code-mix at all
target_learners: young bilingual children aged 2-4 with uneven bilingual first language development
target_learning_goals: syntactic development in two first languages
examples: The model was tested against longitudinal data from five Swedish-French/Italian children, comparing syntactic constituents in monolingual and mixed utterances in each recording
key_sources: Bernardini, P., & Schlyter, S. (2004). Growing syntactic structure and code-mixing in the weaker language: The Ivy Hypothesis. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 7(1), 49-69. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728904001270

article_title: An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom
citation: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4
title: Fully preprogrammed immersive virtual reality (IVR) classroom simulating a computational thinking lesson
description: The article's IVR classroom is a 15-min simulated sixth-grade lesson on computational thinking (coding, sequences, loops), delivered via head-mounted displays to individual students in groups of up to 10. The lesson was "a fully preprogrammed simulation of a typical teaching situation based on audio recordings and motion captures stemming from a real classroom", with 24 virtual classmates whose hand-raising proportion (20/35/65/80%) was manipulated. The element works as an experimental apparatus preserving classroom authenticity while allowing strict control of social comparison information.
requirements: Requires head-mounted displays with noise-canceling headphones and technically reliable hardware; the study excluded 28 participants because of technical issues
constraints: Participants were asked to remain seated and quiet, and the lesson content assumes students have little to no prior computational thinking knowledge
target_learning_goals: basic principles of computational thinking, including coding, sequences, and loops
examples: Groups of up to 10 students at their own schools each experienced the identical IVR lesson in a virtual classroom resembling a blank-slate first-day class.
key_sources: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4

article_title: Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning
citation: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9
title: Theory-driven classification of six IVR learning processes and nine eye-trackable constructs
description: The article develops a classification mapping eye-tracking metrics onto learning processes in IVR, grounded in CTML, CATLM, CASTLE, CAMIL, and Cognitive Load Theory. It proposes "a classification of six key learning processes (i.e., cognitive, motivational, affective, social, metacognitive, media-specific) and nine associated constructs (i.e., attention, visual strategy, cognitive load, motivation, emotion, social attention, self-regulation, immersion, usability) measurable through eye tracking in IVR." The media-specific category was added to capture IVR-specific processes such as embodiment, and review literature supplied the construct subcategories used as the coding scheme.
requirements: Eye-tracking indicators must be matched to constructs via established classifications of fixation-, saccade-, pupil-, blink-, AOI-based, and combined measures
constraints: Classification was developed for IVR delivered through head-mounted displays; AR, MR, and desktop virtual environments were excluded
target_learners: IVR learners across professional, medical, and educational training contexts
target_learning_goals: Assessing cognitive, motivational, affective, social, metacognitive, and media-specific learning processes in IVR
examples: The classification was applied as the coding scheme for a systematic review of 38 empirical IVR eye-tracking studies
key_sources: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9

article_title: Immersive virtual reality–based manual therapy training: a mixed-methods trial
citation: Trinidad-Fernández, M., Bossavit, B., Fuentes-Abolafio, I. J., García-Conejo, C., Mayorga-Vega, D., Díaz-Balboa, E., & Cuesta-Vargas, A. (2026). Immersive virtual reality–based manual therapy training: a mixed-methods trial. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10620-3
title: iVR application for femorotibial mobilization training on Meta Quest 2
description: An immersive virtual reality application developed for the Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display to teach the femorotibial mobilization technique. Users are immersed "with a first-person perspective" in a virtual clinician's room with an articulated supine patient avatar, interacting with the patient's left leg through controllers represented as virtual hands. The application includes a tutorial phase with step-by-step visual guidance and a practice phase with feedback on cadence, aiming to provide "a safe and controlled environment where users can learn and practice the Femorotibial mobilization technique".
requirements: Requires a Meta Quest 2 headset with two manual controllers, whose position and orientation data are used to compute movements following physical principles.
constraints: The application provides no haptic feedback, so tissue deformation and limb weight cannot be felt in the virtual experience.
target_learning_goals: Performing the femorotibial mobilization technique with coordinated angulation and translation movements
key_sources: Trinidad-Fernández, M., Bossavit, B., Fuentes-Abolafio, I. J., García-Conejo, C., Mayorga-Vega, D., Díaz-Balboa, E., & Cuesta-Vargas, A. (2026). Immersive virtual reality–based manual therapy training: a mixed-methods trial. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10620-3

article_title: Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers’ professional vision
citation: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4
title: IVR-based PVAS: an immersive virtual reality assessment system for student teachers' professional vision
description: The IVR-based PVAS is an IVR technology-based professional vision assessment system built in Unity 3D that simulates a middle school classroom with 20 virtual students. Participants act as the instructor, look around freely from a first-person perspective via an HMD, click on students whose behaviour concerns them (perception subtask), and select multiple-choice reasons for misbehaviour while optionally consulting a virtual tablet of student backgrounds (interpretation subtask). The system records fields of view, clicking actions, and log data, and administers a mental effort rating scale after each event. The article states it was developed 'through a design-based research (DBR) approach' across four phases with an expert group.
requirements: An HMD and two Oculus Touch controllers; a backend script editing system for positioning virtual students and editing classroom events
constraints: The classroom scenario represents only one relatively representative type among many possible classroom situations rather than encompassing all types of classroom settings
target_learning_goals: professional vision: perceiving and interpreting student misbehaviour for classroom management
examples: Twenty-four student teachers were assessed on seven classroom events involving three distraction-related misbehaviours, two instructional situations, five seat positions, and four student backgrounds
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2025). Development and implementation of an IVR-based assessment system for student teachers' professional vision. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10463-4

article_title: Immersive virtual reality serious games for evacuation training and research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://www.scopus.com
title: Conceptual framework for developing and implementing IVR serious games for evacuation research
description: The review's main outcome is a conceptual framework (Figure 4) integrating the factors identified across the 15 reviewed papers: expected pedagogical and behavioral outcomes, IVR equipment selection (HMD or PBD) and navigation solutions, development elements (simulated hazards, narrative methods, senses stimulation, NPCs), and an implementation phase in which outcomes and participation experience are measured. The framework "integrates critical aspects and provides connections between them, including pedagogical and behavioral impacts, gaming environment development, and outcome and participation experience measures". It prescribes iterating improvement until measured results meet expectations.
requirements: Researchers need to identify expected outcomes and impacts before the development process
The IVR SGs development needs to include data recording function if such data is necessary for learning measures
Appropriate navigation solution should be designed thoroughly in accordance with the available IVR equipment
constraints: The framework was derived from only 15 eligible papers, twelve of which were rated 6 or over on the review's quality scale
target_learners: building occupants training for indoor emergencies such as fire and earthquake
examples: The framework connects teaching-method selection to participants' background and game narrative method, and links static hazards to the surroundings-driven narrative method
key_sources: Zhenan Feng, Vicente A. González, Robert Amor, Ruggiero Lovreglio, Guillermo Cabrera-Guerrero. (2018). Immersive Virtual Reality Serious Games for Evacuation Training and Research: A Systematic Literature Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.09.002

article_title: Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing
citation: Yizhen Huang, Eric Richter, Thilo Kleickmann, Katharina Scheiter, Dirk Richter. (2023). Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104912
title: Immersive virtual reality classroom with concurrent motion and eye tracking
description: A standardized IVR classroom environment with 30 virtual student agents arranged in five rows and three columns, programmed to display on-task and off-task behaviors. Participants taught through an HTC Vive Pro Eye headset that records eye movements at 120Hz and tracks participant location each second. The article states IVR allows researchers to "track their movement and eye movement unobtrusively and accurately" while maintaining "a balance between realism and standardization of the classroom environment."
requirements: Requires IVR hardware capable of concurrent body and eye movement tracking
constraints: Environmental influences are controlled by standardization, limiting generalizability to real-life classrooms
target_learning_goals: Teacher visual attention to classroom events
key_sources: Yizhen Huang, Eric Richter, Thilo Kleickmann, Katharina Scheiter, Dirk Richter. (2023). Body in motion, attention in focus: A virtual reality study on teachers' movement patterns and noticing. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104912

article_title: Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills
citation: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2021). Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2021.107025
title: IVR River Crossing Game for problem-solving practice
description: An IVR adaptation of the River Crossing Game created for the study using an HTC Vive head-mounted display and handheld controllers. The participant becomes the farmer in the game, controlling the boat directly, unlike the board game and tablet versions where the participant directs the game from outside. The authors state "the participant becomes the farmer in the game, allowing the participant to control the boat and making him or her part of the game".
requirements: An HTC Vive headset with handheld controllers and a dedicated physical space of 4 m × 4 m
constraints: Only one control was used to enable the participant to interact with the environment
key_sources: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2021). Immersive virtual reality as a tool to learn problem-solving skills. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104121

article_title: Immersive procedural training in virtual reality: A systematic literature review
citation: Jongbloed, J., Chaker, R., & Lavoué, E. (2024). Immersive procedural training in virtual reality: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education, 221, 105124. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105124
title: Corpus of 33 peer-reviewed IVR procedural-training studies (2013–2023) with categorized environments, designs, and outcome measures
description: The review assembles a corpus of 33 studies (23 measuring procedural learning outcomes) published between January 2013 and March 2023, identified via PRISMA-guided search of six databases. Studies are categorized into design/usability studies, media comparisons, and value-added research; environments into 360° video, serious games, and simulations; and outcomes into knowledge gain, retention, and transfer. Medicine dominates (twelve studies), and most environments were simulations (22 studies).
requirements: Studies must use an HMD in at least one experimental condition and measure a procedural learning outcome or user-evaluated presence/immersion
constraints: Only media-comparison studies with quantitative outcomes and available descriptive statistics were eligible for the meta-analysis; two studies were excluded for inaccessible statistics
target_learners: Adult professional trainees in medicine, emergency response, industry, aviation, and related domains
target_learning_goals: Procedural knowledge, skill performance, and transfer
key_sources: Jongbloed, J., Chaker, R., & Lavoué, E. (2024). Immersive procedural training in virtual reality: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education, 221, 105124. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105124

article_title: Effects of Head Start Hours on Children's Cognitive, Pre-Academic, and Behavioral Outcomes: An Instrumental Variable Analysis
citation: Li, W., Farkas, G., Duncan, G. J., Vandell, D. L., & Burchinal, M. (2013). Effects of Head Start hours on children's cognitive, pre-academic, and behavioral outcomes: An instrumental variable analysis. SREE Spring 2013 Conference.
title: Instrumental variable approach using center-offered hours to estimate causal effects of Head Start hours on child outcomes
description: The article uses a two-stage least squares instrumental variable approach to address selection bias in estimating effects of Head Start hours. Hours per day offered by Head Start centers serve as instruments for hours per day children actually attend, exploiting variance generated by the HSIS random assignment. Because the instrument is not correlated with family and child characteristics, the second-stage regression yields the estimated effect of hours on child outcomes. Cubic regressions were added to detect non-linear effects.
requirements: Random assignment generating variance in center attendance, as in the HSIS
Center-offered hours as an instrument correlated with attended hours but not with unobserved child and family characteristics
constraints: The analysis may not include control variables only if the random assignment was implemented perfectly; controls were included to adjust for departures from random assignment
target_learners: Low-income preschool children applying to Head Start
target_learning_goals: Estimating causal effects of educational dosage on cognitive, pre-academic, and behavioral outcomes
examples: First-stage F-statistics of hours offered in Head Start centers were above 600, ensuring sufficient instrument-generated variance.
key_sources: Li, W., Farkas, G., Duncan, G. J., Vandell, D. L., & Burchinal, M. (2013). Effects of Head Start hours on children's cognitive, pre-academic, and behavioral outcomes: An instrumental variable analysis. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563041

article_title: The impact of immersive virtual reality training in thyroid surgery: a prospective randomized controlled trial.
citation: Basios Anestis, Voloudakis Nikolaos, Atmatzidis Stefanos, Velikoudi Maria, Bellou Evangelia, Vamvakidis Kyriakos, Papaziogas Basileios, Koutelidakis Ioannis. (2025). The impact of immersive virtual reality training in thyroid surgery: a prospective randomized controlled trial. Updates in Surgery 77(8):2535–2543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-025-02387-8
title: Dedicated immersive VR application for the first steps of open thyroidectomy (MetaQuest3, OramaVR)
description: A dedicated immersive VR training application commissioned by the Hellenic Society of Endocrine Glands Surgery and designed by OramaVR Inc., run on a MetaQuest3 head-mounted display with haptic controllers. It "illustrated specific steps in thyroidectomy including neck incision, dissection of the subcutaneous tissue, creation of sub-platysma flaps, middle line dissection, vagus nerve dissection and placement of a continuous intraoperative neuromonitoring (C-IONM) electrode on the vagus nerve". Residents had to complete the process at least once but could resume training as long as they wished.
requirements: A MetaQuest3 VR device with head-mounted display and haptic controllers; the application covers only the first steps of thyroidectomy, so trainees must also receive instruction on the remainder of the procedure.
constraints: The application was developed only for the first steps of thyroidectomy, so the deducted conclusions cannot be addressed for the whole procedure; haptic feedback was suboptimal for tissue interaction.
target_learners: General surgery residents with at least 6 months of residency training
target_learning_goals: Technical steps of open thyroidectomy from neck incision to continuous intraoperative neuromonitoring electrode placement, including instrument knowledge and flow of operation
examples: In the trial, IVR-group residents trained a mean of 39 ± 8.9 min and repeated the module a median of 3.5 times before performing the steps in the operating room the next day.
key_sources: Basios Anestis, Voloudakis Nikolaos, Atmatzidis Stefanos, Velikoudi Maria, Bellou Evangelia, Vamvakidis Kyriakos, Papaziogas Basileios, Koutelidakis Ioannis. (2025). The impact of immersive virtual reality training in thyroid surgery: a prospective randomized controlled trial. Updates in Surgery 77(8):2535–2543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-025-02387-8

article_title: The effectiveness of immersive virtual reality as a student-centered tool for learning neuroanatomy: A single-blind randomized controlled trial with physiotherapy students.
citation: García‐Robles P, Obrero‐Gaitán E, Cortés‐Pérez I, Ibancos‐Losada MdR, Díaz‐Fernández Á, Osuna‐Pérez MC. (2025). The effectiveness of immersive virtual reality as a student‐centered tool for learning neuroanatomy: A single‐blind randomized controlled trial with physiotherapy students. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70068
title: Use immersive VR as a complementary, student‐centered intervention for teaching neuroanatomy to physiotherapy students
description: The authors advocate adding IVR sessions alongside traditional teaching within a student‐centered learning approach: "our findings advocate for the inclusion of IVR devices as a complementary intervention within a SCL approach to teaching neuroanatomy to physiotherapy students." IVR supports autonomous manipulation of 3D anatomical models, which the authors link to customized, interactive learning and to developing the three‐dimensional organization of brain areas needed for clinical transfer.
requirements: Used as a supplement to, not replacement for, didactic lectures
Instructor familiarization session on the hardware and software before autonomous use
constraints: Advantages were demonstrated only in the short term; differences were not maintained at 4 weeks after a single 90‐minute session
Assessment tools were ad‐hoc without reliability and validity values
target_learning_goals: neuroanatomy knowledge acquisition and three‐dimensional structural understanding
examples: In the trial, both groups received the same lecture, then the IVR group studied autonomously with Meta Quest 2 and Sharecare YOU VR while the control group used the Prometheus Atlas of Anatomy
key_sources: García‐Robles P, Obrero‐Gaitán E, Cortés‐Pérez I, Ibancos‐Losada MdR, Díaz‐Fernández Á, Osuna‐Pérez MC. (2025). The effectiveness of immersive virtual reality as a student‐centered tool for learning neuroanatomy: A single‐blind randomized controlled trial with physiotherapy students. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70068

article_title: Intraoperative fluoroscopy skills in distal radius fracture surgery: valid and reliable assessment on a novel immersive virtual reality simulator.
citation: Sønderup M, Gustafsson A, Konge L, Jacobsen M E. (2024). Intraoperative fluoroscopy skills in distal radius fracture surgery: valid and reliable assessment on a novel immersive virtual reality simulator. Acta Orthopaedica 95: 477–484. https://doi.org/10.2340/17453674.2024.41345
title: Immersive virtual reality simulator for intraoperative fluoroscopy training in distal radius fracture surgery
description: An immersive VR simulator developed with software developer VitaSim, consisting of an Oculus Quest 2 head-mounted display connected to a laptop with two handheld controllers, immersing the user in an operating room with a C-arm fluoroscopy unit and a patient who has undergone volar plating surgery. Ray-tracing technology in Unity creates "realistic fluoroscopy images ... depending on the position of the wrist relative to the fluoroscopy machine". Users transfer five pre-defined fluoroscopic views from a global Delphi consensus study, and angular values, image counts, and completion time are automatically recorded. The article states the simulator "enables practice without exposure to radiation or compromising patient safety".
requirements: A head-mounted display, laptop, and two handheld controllers; the simulator automatically records angular values, image counts, and task time for scoring
constraints: Limb movement is restricted to 3 axes at the elbow and wrist; the scenario covers only fluoroscopy control of an already completed surgery; the C-arm automatically centers, eliminating causes of unclear images such as hand tremor; only the operator is present, omitting a radiographer as required in some countries
target_learners: Orthopedic surgeons in trauma or hand surgery
target_learning_goals: Intraoperative fluoroscopic image acquisition and assessment after volar locking plate fixation of distal radius fractures
examples: Participants performed 3 repetitions of a complete intraoperative fluoroscopy control consisting of all 5 images per session, across 2 sessions with a minimum of 4 weeks between sessions
key_sources: Sønderup M, Gustafsson A, Konge L, Jacobsen M E. (2024). Intraoperative fluoroscopy skills in distal radius fracture surgery: valid and reliable assessment on a novel immersive virtual reality simulator. Acta Orthopaedica 95: 477–484. https://doi.org/10.2340/17453674.2024.41345

article_title: Teaching ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheter placement through immersive virtual reality: An explorative pilot study.
citation: Andersen NL, Jensen RO, Posth S, Laursen CB, Jørgensen R, Graumann O. (2021). Teaching ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheter placement through immersive virtual reality: An explorative pilot study. Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8270624/
title: IVR training scenario progression pattern: decreasing vessel size and increasing depth across repeated practice scenarios
description: The IVR training used a structured progression pattern across its 10 virtual scenarios: "All 10 scenarios were similarly structured but they increased in difficulty, with the size of the vessel decreasing while its depth increased." Each scenario required the student to place a PVC in a deep vein visible only via US using a cross-sectional scanning plane and tip tracking, then press an evaluate position button for feedback before proceeding. This graduated difficulty structure allowed repeated practice of the same core skill under increasingly demanding conditions.
requirements: Scenarios must be similarly structured so the core tip tracking skill remains constant while difficulty parameters change
constraints: Pattern was implemented within a single IVR simulator session of approximately 20 minutes total; no phantoms were used in the simulation
target_learners: Medical students novices to US-guided procedures
target_learning_goals: Tip tracking and PVC placement competency in deep veins visible only via ultrasound
examples: The IVR group trained on 10 scenarios where vessel size decreased and depth increased, then was assessed on a phantom with 3 PVCs of increasing gauge size (18G, 16G, 14G)
key_sources: Andersen NL, Jensen RO, Posth S, Laursen CB, Jørgensen R, Graumann O. (2021). Teaching ultrasound-guided peripheral venous catheter placement through immersive virtual reality: An explorative pilot study. Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8270624/

article_title: Successful mLearning Pilot in Senegal: Delivering Family Planning Refresher Training Using Interactive Voice Response and SMS.
citation: Diedhiou A, Gilroy KE, Cox CM, Duncan L, Koumtingue D, Pacqué-Margolis S, Fort A, Settle D, Bailey R. (2015). Successful mLearning Pilot in Senegal: Delivering Family Planning Refresher Training Using Interactive Voice Response and SMS. Global Health: Science and Practice. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-14-00220
title: IVR mLearning system combining interactive voice response, SMS prompts, and spaced education on simple mobile phones
description: A prototype mLearning system built on open source technologies (FreeSWITCH for voice, Gammu for SMS, Moodle for quiz management) that delivered audio-recorded multiple choice questions and explanations to any type of phone. Participants received a daily SMS prompt, texted back when ready, and answered questions via telephone keypad, hearing detailed explanations after each answer. The course used "a spaced-education approach in which questions and detailed explanations are spaced and repeated over time", retiring questions after two correct answers.
requirements: Participants need a simple mobile phone with network reception; the system requires a telephony platform, SMS modem, and quiz management software
A 3-hour orientation prepared participants to use the system
constraints: The medium does not permit clinical practice, demonstrations, instructor interaction, or display of images such as diagrams and graphs
Reliability of cellular networks in remote areas remains a challenge
target_learners: public-sector nurses and midwives in Senegal
target_learning_goals: management of contraceptive side effects and misconceptions
examples: Used to deliver an 8-week refresher course aligned with the Senegal family planning national training curriculum to 20 health workers in Thiès region
key_sources: Diedhiou A, Gilroy KE, Cox CM, Duncan L, Koumtingue D, Pacqué-Margolis S, Fort A, Settle D, Bailey R. (2015). Successful mLearning Pilot in Senegal: Delivering Family Planning Refresher Training Using Interactive Voice Response and SMS. Global Health: Science and Practice. https://doi.org/10.9745/GHSP-D-14-00220
